articles.title: Appeals panel wrestles with block of RFK Jr.’s vaccine panel appointments
articles.summary: The Trump administration told a federal appeals panel Tuesday that a lower court erred in blocking Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s handpicked appointees from serving on a key vaccine advisory panel. Justice Department attorney Matthew Zorn told the 1st U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals that a district court judge did not have the authority to…
articles.body:
The Trump administration told a federal appeals panel Tuesday that a lower court erred in blocking Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s handpicked appointees from serving on a key vaccine advisory panel.

Justice Department attorney Matthew Zorn told the 1 st U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals that a district court judge did not have the authority to suspend Kennedy’s appointments to the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP).

Zorn said the practical effect of the lower court’s ruling is that ACIP has been blocked from meeting in any capacity. Even if Kennedy tried to appoint new members, or followed a different procedure, Zorn said those moves would be blocked.

“The secretary wants to get the ACIP back to work, and we are being told if he reconstitutes any committee, it’s going to be right back in court,” Zorn said.

ACIP makes recommendations on vaccine policy to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), which help determine which shots are covered through private and government health insurance programs.

Judge Brian Murphy of the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts ruled in March that Kennedy likely violated federal procedures when he fired all 17 members of ACIP and selected new panelists, many of whom shared his skepticism of vaccines.

Murphy ruled Kennedy picked “distinctly unqualified” individuals instead of experts on vaccines and immunization and disregarded the scientific process that historically underpinned the committee’s work.

Some of the judges on the appeals panel appeared puzzled about the lower court’s ruling, questioning why it seemed Murphy made no legal explanation for blocking Kennedy’s appointees.

The plaintiffs argued that Murphy’s ruling doesn’t prevent Kennedy from appointing a new ACIP. He just needs to follow the law’s requirements of fair balance and expertise for panelists.

They said the administration wants to use the same unlawful process to reconstitute ACIP with members who will support Kennedy’s quest to roll back childhood vaccines.

Over the course of three meetings prior to Murphy’s ruling, Kennedy’s ACIP rescinded several recommendations for childhood shots, including the immunization of all newborns against hepatitis B.

Murphy temporarily blocked the appointments, as well as other changes to the vaccine schedule made by ACIP and Kennedy, while the lawsuit plays out.

The lawsuit was filed by the American Academy of Pediatrics and other medical groups seeking to stop Kennedy from scaling back of the nation’s childhood vaccination schedule.

The lawsuit was originally focused on Kennedy’s decision to stop recommending COVID-19 vaccinations for most children and pregnant women, but it was amended as Kennedy and the Department of Health and Human Services took additional steps that they argued undermined pediatric vaccines.

For instance, Kennedy bypassed ACIP and unilaterally announced a new childhood vaccine schedule, effectively reducing the number of diseases against which children are routinely immunized to 11 from 17.

The Trump administration did not appeal the lower court’s pause of Kennedy’s changes to the immunization schedule. Instead, the government focused on ACIP.

images.caption: Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. speaks during a news conference on the Autism report by the CDC at the Hubert Humphrey Building Auditorium in Washington, April 16, 2025.

articles.title: Trump: Government will take massive stake in ‘next generation’ submarine shipyard
articles.summary: President Trump said Tuesday that American taxpayers will get a 40 percent stake in the planned shipyard in Sparrows Point, Md., an unincorporated industrial area in Baltimore County, which he visited Tuesday. “In the ultimate proof of our commitment to ensuring shipyards enduring success American taxpayers will receive 40 percent stake in the new shipyard,”…
articles.body:
President Trump said Tuesday that American taxpayers will get a 40 percent stake in the planned shipyard in Sparrows Point, Md., an unincorporated industrial area in Baltimore County, which he visited Tuesday.

“In the ultimate proof of our commitment to ensuring shipyards enduring success American taxpayers will receive 40 percent stake in the new shipyard,” Trump said.

“We get 40 percent and the storied grounds of Sparrow’s Point will never fall silent again,” he continued. “There’s a tremendous amount of activity going on.”

Defense contractor Anduril is planning to invest $3.7 billion in the new shipyard to manufacture parts for Virginia-class submarines. The company secured up to a $2.9 billion contract with the U.S. Navy to help establish the facility, a 2 million square-foot project to be dubbed Arsenal-2.

Virginia-class submarines are nuclear-powered attack submarines that have vertical launching system-launched cruise missile capability. Efforts to build the submarines have been hampered by not having enough experienced workers, and the late delivery of materials, according to a July report from the Government Accountability Office (GAO).

Trump, who is seeking to tout his efforts on the economy amid polls that suggest Republicans are in for a tough midterm election next month because of souring voter moods on affordability, touted the project as part of $21 trillion being invested into the U.S. He said it would create 3,000 jobs in Maryland.

“But we are doing like no country has ever done: $21 trillion. And we’re building plants. We’re building everything,” he said.

Under the Trump administration, Washington’s portfolio has grown to include stakes in over 30 companies , including a 9.9 percent stake in Intel and 10 percent direct ownership of Trilogy Metals.

images.caption: President Trump gives an address at Anduril Industries in Sparrows Point, Md., on Tuesday, October 9, 2026. Anduril Industries is investing $3.7 billion to construct a new shipbuilding facility named Arsenal 2.

articles.title: Trump spent over $10M in taxpayer cash on ads critics likened to North Korean 'propaganda' — now his super PAC will pay
articles.summary: “If President Trump wants people to love him, he can pay for it himself,” Senate and House Democrats say.
articles.body:
If President Donald Trump orders any new promotional ads decrying "deep state" enemies alongside images like fighter plane flyovers or Mount Rushmore or even Trump himself, he'll be paying for them out of his own pocket.

The tax breaks in Trump's 'big beautiful bill' expire after 2028. Here are 4 moves to make before the window closes

Jeff Bezos backs a platform that lets anyone invest in rental homes for as little as $100 — 6 ways to build wealth like a landlord without actually being one

Dave Ramsey warns nearly 50% of Americans are making 1 big Social Security mistake. Here's what it is and 3 simple steps to fix it ASAP

On Monday, Trump seemed to bow to political pressure over using taxpayer funds to pay for his promotional ads — which have included elements of the president's 2024 campaign messaging — announcing on Truth Social: "I have decided to do the Patriotic Ads, among others, and pay for them myself, and with money I raised for MAGA, Inc."

On Tuesday, per the New York Times, a White House spokesperson noted that Trump's announcement "was not referring to reimbursement ."

Congressional critics have characterized the ads as "the sort of government propaganda one might expect in North Korea," while Trump, via the Department of Homeland Security, has reportedly already spent more than $10 million in taxpayer dollars on them. The ads run the disclaimer "Paid for by the U.S. government."

CNN, meanwhile, noted that Trump's team created "at least 13 campaign-style ads," including three "highlighting the US military and operations in Iran and Venezuela" and another dubbed "God Made Trump," which haven't aired yet.

A White House spokesperson told Moneywise that Trump's turnabout on using taxpayer dollars "was not referring to reimbursement," adding that "presidential public service announcements are nothing new. Administrations of both parties have used public service announcements to explain policy and make the case for the nation's direction."

Blurring the line between public service and personal promotion

A joint letter from Senate and House Democrats to the White House in September called out one ad that "celebrates President Trump with a montage of photos of him and the American flag as singers repeat the words 'love me' from JMSN's song 'Love Me.'"

They continued, "If President Trump wants people to love him, he can pay for it himself," adding, "The law is not complicated. You cannot use taxpayer dollars for political advertisements."

articles.title: Plague in Russia sparks concern, COVID-19 pandemic memories: 5 things to know
articles.summary: The death of Russian lab technician researching the plague has set off alarms abroad and at home as observers note resemblances to the conditions that some theorized preceded the COVID-19 pandemic. Reports emerged last week that a laboratory worker at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East had died shortly after being hospitalized. The news…
articles.body:
The death of Russian lab technician researching the plague has set off alarms abroad and at home as observers note resemblances to the conditions that some theorized preceded the COVID-19 pandemic.

Reports emerged last week that a laboratory worker at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East had died shortly after being hospitalized.

The news put the international community on high alert, with the U.S. reaching out to offer assistance. Though Russian authorities have so far downplayed the seriousness of the incident.

The World Health Organization (WHO) said it asked Russian authorities on Oct. 3 for information to assess the risk, receiving a response soon after denying reports the lab worker had caught the deadly disease.

The infection and death occurring in close proximity to a laboratory researching infectious diseases is evoking concerns of another potential outbreak like that of COVID-19, though the origins of that pandemic have still yet to be determined.

Here are five things to know about the situation in Russia.

Igor Kobzev, governor of the Irkutsk region, said on a Russian social media platform that the employee had died of “pneumonia of unknown etiology” — adding that no pathogens linked to their work were detected in samples taken from the patient. No other employees have reported illnesses in the past 10 days.

Local media have identified the laboratory worker as 28-year-old Darya Shipilova, though Russian authorities have yet to confirm this.

According to Kobzev, individuals who had contact with the research institute worker have been identified, examined and are currently under medical observation — involving daily laboratory testing.

The Moscow Times reported that nearly 200 people are currently under medical observation following his death. The outlet cited Russian media reporting that the laboratory worker had told hospital staff that she had accidentally broken a test tube containing live bacteria.

Th plague is a disease caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis. In the modern day, it is often associated with The Black Plague that spread throughout Europe in the 14th century.

Bubonic plague and pneumonic plague are caused by the same bacteria, with the latter developing when bubonic plague goes untreated. The term “bubonic” refers to bubos, or swollen lymph nodes, that are caused by plague infections , while pneumonic refers to the pneumonia-like illness it can progress to.

Jeanne Marrazzo , CEO of the Infectious Diseases Society of America , told The Hill plague infections are easily treatable today with common antibiotics like ciprofloxacin.

“You can treat that, and people do fine. It’s not like it’s a death sentence. It doesn’t mean it’s going to go septic,” said Marrazzo, who formerly led the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID).

“It can go IV septic, which means it sort of goes crazy across the body, and that’s when people really get into trouble. But it only happens about 10 percent of the time,” she added. “The really scary thing is the is the pneumonic form of the disease, and this is when you directly inhale it.”

The plague is rarely transmitted from person-to-person, but when it becomes pneumonic and reaches a person’s lungs, that is when it can spread through such interactions. An incubation period for the infection can be less than a day.

Marrazzo emphasized that the current risk to Americans is extremely low, noting that people are much more likely to be infected by a seasonal respiratory virus than the plague at this time.

President Trump responded to news of the laboratory worker’s death in Russia, calling pneumonic plague a “rough disease” and saying the U.S. would assist the country if needed.

“I hate to see them having it,” Trump told reporters. “Anybody that has that kind of a problem, we’re always willing to help.”

The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) said in a statement Monday that it is “closely monitoring the situation.”

“Based on the limited information currently available, there are no reports of secondary cases and no evidence of sustained human-to-human transmission that would cause further spread of the disease,” the ECDC noted.

Russia’s Central Asian neighbors — including Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan and Tajikistan — have implemented closer border checks on people on entering their countries in response to the death.

As NIAID’s past director, Marrazzo said she expects her former agency is “all hands on deck” determining how to handle the plague case.

“We would be on the phone nonstop as much as we could or needed to be with our international partners, because you’ve seen some reassuring comments from WHO and some other people, and that’s really who you would expect to be fronting their response in this case,” Marrazzo said.

While Russia responded promptly to its inquiries, the WHO said in a statement that it is seeking more information on the situation in Irkutsk.

“WHO has requested additional information from Russia on which pneumonia-causing pathogen led to the woman’s death. WHO is following the situation closely, keeping other countries informed, and ready to support the Russian authorities if they ask,” the WHO said.

314 Action, a political action committee dedicated to getting Democratic scientists into office, called on Trump to demand more transparency from Russian President Vladimir Putin following the plague death.

“If this administration is serious about protecting Americans, Trump and Rubio should demand full transparency from the Russian government instead of rolling out the welcome mat for war criminal Vladimir Putin at the G20 in Miami. We don’t know what this is, but they do,” 314 Action President Shaughnessy Naughton sa i d in a statement.

While in Iceland, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said at a press conference, ” I think it’s incumbent upon Russia to obviously share more information with the world. That’s what they should do. That’s what we hope they will do. And the more we can learn about what happened, then the better all of us can be in a position of responding.”

Public health experts are weary of what Russian authorities are conveying to the global community about what happened at the lab in Irkutsk.

“It’s always good to have a high index of suspicion when you’re dealing with places that don’t have a great track record for being open and transparent about what’s going on,” said Marrazzo.

“They really have not always been very open about what these kinds of situations are. What’s the epidemiology? Where are things happening? And so that really does make people very anxious,” she said of Russia. “And I think I think it’s justified because you don’t often see Russian scientists presenting at major meetings where many people go to exchange updates on the epidemiology of current outbreaks.”

Ashish Jha, senior fellow at the Harvard Kennedy School’s Belfer Center and former White House COVID-19 response coordinator, cited the country’s past record of obscuring the truth of public health outbreaks as cause for questioning Russia’s answers.

“People who have been in contact with a pneumonic plague patient normally receive prophylactic antibiotics, not lockdowns or the involvement of security services. This raises serious questions about what happened inside the lab,” he wrote in a Tuesday op-ed for The Boston Globe . “In 1979, anthrax spores escaped from a military facility in Sverdlovsk, and more than 60 people died. For 13 years, Soviet authorities blamed the deaths on contaminated meat.”

images.caption: FILE – In this Aug. 10, 2019 file photo, a sign warning of bubonic plague is displayed at a parking lot near the Rocky Mountain Arsenal Wildlife Refuge in Commerce City, Colo. The bacteria which causes the disease is transmitted through the bites of infected fleas, which spread it between rodents, pets and humans. (AP Photo/David Zalubowski)

articles.title: World Faces Risk Cocktail From AI, Oil and Debt, Says IMF Chief
articles.summary: Global governments must act urgently to address challenges from an unbalanced AI boom, a prolonged energy shock and record debt piles, the International Mone...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Global governments must act urgently to address challenges from an unbalanced AI boom, a prolonged energy shock and record debt piles, the International Monetary Fund said as it prepares to host economy chiefs from around the world next week.

The rush to develop artificial intelligence is delivering a growth spurt that's so far confined to a handful of countries, Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said Wednesday in prepared remarks in Singapore ahead of the annual IMF-World Bank meetings in Bangkok next week.

Meantime the squeeze on key commodity supplies due to conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine is set to continue into 2027, and soaring bond yields have left governments that amassed too much debt under mounting budget pressure, Georgieva said — calling advanced economies the "worst offenders" on the latter count.

"The AI building boom is inflationary. The energy and food shocks are inflationary. Tariffs, defense spending, and high public debt can be inflationary," Georgieva said. She called for a "prudently hawkish bias" on the part of central banks, and said countries that have gotten used to running large budget deficits are in for "some very tough political choices."

The weeklong Bangkok gathering of top finance ministers and central bank governors takes place against a backdrop of turbulence in sovereign debt markets, as yields on US, European and Japanese bonds hit multi-decade highs. Total global debt has now surpassed $365 trillion, according to the Institute of International Finance.

"Policymakers had a relatively easy ride over the last 17 years as for all that time interest rates were stuck below GDP growth rates," Georgieva said. "Higher interest rates now put an end to that."

By contrast, the wave of AI investment — and expectations for the economic gains it will deliver — keeps propeling stocks to new highs, and has delivered record exports for Asia's powerhouse producers of chips and other equipment.

The bond selloff got underway after the US and Israel attacked Iran in February, choking off fuel supplies and raising costs worldwide. Georgieva said the energy shock has been "large but contained" so far. But she warned that "price pressures may build further as demand rises with the approach of the Northern hemisphere cold season and as countries replenish reserves."

images.caption: Kristalina Georgieva · Bloomberg · Bloomberg

articles.title: Takaichi Says Japan May Review Spending if Yields Move Sharply
articles.summary: Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said her administration is prepared to review spending and revenue plans if government bond yields move unexpectedly,...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said her administration is prepared to review spending and revenue plans if government bond yields move unexpectedly, as she seeks parliamentary support for a temporary cut to the tax on food sales.

"Should market conditions such as yields move unexpectedly, we will take policy measures such as restructuring various initiatives and reviewing expenditures and revenues," she said on Wednesday in response to questions during a parliamentary session.

"If situations arise that significantly impact Japan's economy, such as disruptions in the global economy, we will respond flexibly by utilizing reserve funds," she added. She declined to comment on specific currency or yield levels.

With parliament in session, Takaichi is set to see through a bill that will cut the sales tax on food items and non-alcoholic beverages to 1% from 8% for two years starting in April. She is seeking to alleviate the burden of rising costs on households while trying to convince markets that government finances are sound.

Takaichi's government is set to compile the budget for the year starting April over the next few months. The budget will likely offer insight into whether she can deliver on plans to grow Japan's economy while keeping spending in check. In that time, she will also be tasked with communicating with markets effectively as the yen remains weak and long-term yields trend higher around the globe.

By year-end, Takaichi is also set to overhaul Japan's security documents, which will give hints on the pace and extent to which defense spending may rise over the next several years. Takaichi has already accelerated defense spending to almost 2% of gross domestic product in the financial year that ended in March this year, two years ahead of schedule.

She has not set any numerical targets for defense outlays since, but officials are considering a scenario in which Japan could match the commitment made by South Korea to increase spending to 3.5% of GDP over the next decade.

"We will deepen concrete and realistic deliberations in accordance with our independent judgment, and build up the process accordingly," she said.

articles.title: Why Trump chose these leaders to head his ‘Super Intelligence Force’
articles.summary: President Trump’s selection of four administration officials to head up his new “Super Intelligence Force” is offering a window into how the White House will approach AI in the face of pressure over its risks. The group of government leaders each reflect different priorities of the Trump administration after months of mixed messaging on the…
articles.body:
President Trump’s selection of four administration officials to head up his new “ Super Intelligence Force ” is offering a window into how the White House will approach AI in the face of pressure over its risks.

The group of government leaders each reflect different priorities of the Trump administration after months of mixed messaging on the White House’s AI policy.

Now referring to artificial intelligence as “super intelligence,” the president announced last weekend he tapped Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton to lead the Super Intelligence Force (SIF), which aims to explore the benefits and risks of the technology, and “ensure” America’s lead in the development race.

Clayton will be joined by Emil Michael, the Pentagon’s chief technology officer; Andrew Ferguson, chair of the Federal Trade Commission (FTC); and Scott Kupor, the director of the Office of Personnel Management, to serve as vice chairs .

Here’s what to know about the SIF officials:

Clayton, who became director of national intelligence in August after serving as U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York, has long been praised by Trump, who once described the Cabinet member as a “strong fighter for the truth.”

As national intelligence director, Clayton oversees the U.S.’s 18-agency intelligence community, which is increasingly playing a role in the testing and evaluations of AI systems.

While Clayton has not worked directly in tech, his ties to both the legal world and Wall Street are likely to play a role. Trump previously tapped Clayton, a longtime lawyer, to chair the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) in his first term.

The president said Sunday the group “will coordinate the Federal Government’s engagement with Consumers, Public Interest Groups, Religious Organizations, Critical Infrastructure Providers, and Super Intelligence Companies.”

The White House said the group will have 120 days to report on AI’s risks and benefits, and the role of government in managing it.

After attending the White House’s meeting last week with more than two dozen tech industry executives and administration officials, Clayton doubled down on Trump’s commitment against slowing down AI development.

“To take a pause … in some way, not try to drive forward inside the United States with companies that are regulated in the United States … to somehow say, ‘We should back away from this and let the rest of the world develop these models and implement these models,’ I don’t think anyone in that room, anyone in America should think that’s a good strategy,” Clayton told CNBC , referring to the AI luncheon.

In the wake of multiple incidents of AI models going “rogue” and researchers warning the technology could harm humans, a handful of industry executives like Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman called for a slowdown in development to manage the risks.

Trump dismissed these concerns as a “hoax,” remaining steadfast in his view that the U.S. should charge forward on AI development to stay ahead of China.

Clayton emphasized last week that he sees AI as a “ national security issue ” and kept the door open to government intervention through the Justice Department or the FTC if needed.

Michael, a former Uber executive, currently serves as the undersecretary of Defense for research and engineering. He has taken a hard-line approach to AI, arguing the Pentagon should have expansive authority over how it uses the technology.

He was at the center of the Pentagon’s dispute with Anthropic, repeatedly slamming Claude’s creator over its push to establish safety guardrails in its contract with the Defense Department.

After negotiations with Anthropic fell apart earlier this year, the Pentagon took the rare step of labeling the AI firm a supply chain risk — a designation typically reserved for foreign adversaries. The company challenged the decision in court with mixed results.

Even as Trump and the White House have at times sought to cool tensions with Anthropic, Michael has kept up his adversarial stance toward the company.

After an Anthropic policy official voiced support for an administration official’s criticism of Chinese distillation of U.S. models in July, the Pentagon’s tech chief slammed the firm , arguing there “is no AI company more hostile to the warfighter.”

Like Trump, Michael advocates for a hands-off approach on AI regulation.

“At the @DeptofWar [Department of Defense] we have seen what is possible when red tape is removed and America’s best technology is rapidly put into action,” he wrote on social media after the president tapped him for the task force.

“Working alongside America’s leading technology companies, we are putting the most advanced SI [super intelligence] capabilities into the hands of our warfighters at speed and scale,” he continued.

Ferguson, a former antitrust litigator, represents a contingent of Republicans who often favor light-touch regulations but are much less friendly toward Big Tech on issues around consumer protection or kids’ online safety.

Trump touted Ferguson’s “proven record of standing up to Big Tech censorship” when nominating him as chair of the FTC, one of two agencies tasked with enforcing antitrust laws. This area has increasingly focused on major tech firms in recent years, with Ferguson inheriting cases against both Meta and Amazon.

Despite reported efforts by Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg to settle the case last year, the FTC went forward with a high-profile trial against the social media giant. After a judge found Meta did not have a monopoly, the agency appealed the decision in January.

Ferguson has also sought to crack down on tech companies over kids’ online safety, warning in June 2025 that officials “cannot stand idly by and invoke innovation as a reason not to take steps to protect children.”

The FTC chair has aligned himself with Trump on AI regulations — maintaining the government already has laws on hand to keep the technology in check and warning new rules could allow companies to “build a moat” around themselves.

“It’s not like the government has no tools to protect Americans today,” he told Fox News last month. “We have the product liability laws. We have the consumer protection laws. We have a host of rules that apply to every industry, not just AI.”

While some critics have knocked this approach as ineffective, Ferguson doesn’t appear to be pulling punches. The FTC confirmed last week it is investigating both OpenAI and Anthropic over the potential dangers their models pose to consumers.

Kupor brings nearly three decades of experience in the technology and venture capital spaces, previously working as managing partner at Silicon Valley-based venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz and the web hosting company HP.

As director of the Office of Personnel Management (OPM), Kupor has made the government’s adoption of AI a priority , while emphasizing the technology is not intended to replace humans. He spearheaded OPM’s Tech Force program , a hiring initiative to bring tech talent to the government.

He told Fox Business Network this week the group plans to produce a “comprehensive plan” that both positions the U.S. to stay ahead of China and addresses the risks of the technology.

“Nobody’s going to get a free pass here,” Kupor said. “The question, though, is do you want to make sure you don’t introduce a regulatory scheme that will slow down or impact the ability of the inventiveness of this country to win in what is an incredibly important technology?”

articles.title: Pentagon, under Hegseth, expands war on drug cartels with troops on ground in South America
articles.summary: The Pentagon is expanding the U.S. military’s multifront war against drug cartels in South America. For more than a year, the U.S. military has been blowing up alleged drug boats on both sides of the continent. Forces have also begun interdicting refueling vessels off the coast of Ecuador before destroying them. And recently, U.S. special…
articles.body:
The Pentagon is expanding the U.S. military’s multifront war against drug cartels in South America.

For more than a year, the U.S. military has been blowing up alleged drug boats on both sides of the continent. Forces have also begun interdicting refueling vessels off the coast of Ecuador before destroying them.

And recently, U.S. special forces started embedding on the ground with Ecuadorian authorities in raids against alleged drug traffickers, introducing a new front in the Trump administration’s campaign against criminal groups designated as foreign terrorist organizations.

“Based on our assessment of what needs to be done, this plan focuses on five core lines of effort: dismantling illicit networks, attacking network logistics, preventing adversary regeneration, bolstering partner sovereignty and security, and building a strong coalition,” U.S. Southern Command (Southcom) Commander Gen. Francis L. Donovan said in a recent interview with The Hill when discussing Southcom’s “Offensive Campaign Plan” that addresses regional threats to security and stability.

Since returning to the White House last year, President Trump has pressured drug cartels in the Western Hemisphere, warning that their drug trafficking is directly contributing to the deaths of Americans.

The U.S. has labeled 20 Latin American-based cartels and other criminal groups as foreign terrorist organizations and began kinetic actions across the continent last fall. The administration has also deepened its defense cooperation with countries, establishing the 19-member Americas Counter Cartel Coalition (ACCC) to counter transnational organized crime.

The cooperation has borne fruit in Ecuador, where the government has wanted to aggressively partner with U.S. forces to help take out criminal syndicates such as Los Choneros and Los Lobos, which have ties to Mexico’s Jalisco New Generation Cartel.

Two weeks ago in Ecuador, about 50 U.S. service members and law enforcement personnel took part in raids carried out by Ecuadorean police against alleged drug traffickers.

The U.S. military collaborated with Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) counterparts and the Ecuadorian military in the lead-up to the raids, according to a senior U.S. official.

Going forward, the U.S. special operations forces will help train partner forces to aid in “command and control” operations on the ground, but they “are not on target until the target’s clear,” the senior official said.

“Then we bring our special operations forces with their abilities to do sensitive site exploitation to develop the intelligence for the next operation,” the official said.

Benjamin Gedan, a senior fellow and the director of the Stimson Center Latin America program, said the U.S. in the past has fought organized crime in the region by strengthening criminal justice institutions, including courts, prosecutors and police. He argued today’s Pentagon strategy principally relies on “mislabeling drug gangs as terrorists and blowing things up.”

“That approach generates content for social media, but it will do little to disrupt the drug lords responsible for the mayhem in Latin American communities and the region’s epic struggle with public corruption,” Gedan told The Hill.

Previously, the U.S. has given Ecuador and other allied countries gear, training and intelligence support to go after criminal groups.

The U.S. conducted the first joint operation with Ecuador in early March. The U.S. Southern Command (Southcom) conducted an attack alongside Venezuela that killed a Tren de Aragua gang leader.

Ecuador’s relationship with Washington has evolved and on-the-ground raids will resume.

“That’s kind of like a graduation of how we’ve been able to work with that country, but certainly not the endpoint. Just kind of like progress along the way. So I think you will expect to see more operations, especially as capabilities begin to start to develop,” a senior Pentagon official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss internal military matters, told The Hill on Tuesday.

Guatemala and Honduras have sent letters to the U.S. requesting joint operations, according to the senior Pentagon official.

Former acting DEA Administrator Derek Maltz said the Trump administration has recognized that synthetic drugs have “destroyed” American communities and families at “levels that we’ve never seen in the history” of the U.S.

“A lot of people that seem to think some of these tactics are a little aggressive,” said Maltz, who spent nearly 30 years in law enforcement. “Well, you have to be aggressive against terrorists because they’re destroying our future.”

Maltz said the administration has recognized it needs to decimate the cartels’ supply line, funding streams, operations and manufacturing labs throughout the region. He predicted there soon could be operations inside Colombia, which has been overflowing with cocaine trafficking.

“I would anticipate that they will provide any type of support that the Colombians or Ecuadorians or Hondurans the leadership requests,” he said, calling the U.S. special forces “best in the business.”

Donovan said Southcom’s objective is to apply “total systemic friction” against the narco-terrorists groups.

“To reflect this, we have shifted our terminology from isolated lists of terrorist organizations to hemispheric threat networks. These networks span from the points of origin, such as cocaine production in Colombia or Northern Peru, as well as other illicit activities, and move north toward the United States through Mexico, along the eastern and western coasts, or across the Atlantic and Pacific oceans,” Donovan said in the interview. “We are now actively tracking these alternate logistics flows.”

The U.S. military continues to carry out deadly strikes against alleged drug-trafficking vessels in the Caribbean and Eastern Pacific. American forces have conducted at least 71 strikes and killed 239 people the U.S. alleges are “narco-terrorists” since Sept. 2, 2025.

Critics, including some law-of-war experts, have panned the attacks as summary executions.

Since late August, the U.S. military has zeroed in on another target off the coast of Ecuador — “floating refueling stations” — taking a more humane approach. A helicopter hovers over the water, and U.S. Marines board the large fishing vessel to remove the crew on board, handing them over to Ecuadorian authorities. And then the boat is blown up.

The multifront campaign has curbed the flow of cocaine heading toward the U.S.

The movement of vessels with U.S.-bound cocaine has been reduced between 30 percent and 60 percent in the Eastern Caribbean, Western Caribbean and the two lanes in the Eastern Pacific, south Galapagos and north Galapagos, according to the senior Pentagon official.

Central Caribbean was the only maritime corridor that has seen an increase, and the U.S. is working with the Dominican Republic, Jamaica, the Bahamas and other nations to develop an “island chain of homeland defense” to halt the flow, the official said.

The U.S. is pouring more resources into Latin America as the Trump administration continues executing its pivot to the Americas.

The Pentagon has moved a few MQ-9 Reaper drones, which can cost up to $50 million each, from the U.S. Africa Command to Ecuador and Colombia, the New York Times reported on Tuesday. Southcom declined to comment.

“The U.S. is kind of saying we’re going to provide you with the tools, not only maybe to actually strike at some of these gangs, but really I think first and foremost to surveil your territory and try to identify illicit activity that’s going on, and you have that capability as opposed to going to us,” said Henry Ziemer, a fellow with the Americas Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, adding that Colombia and Ecuador have historically had limited long endurance UAV capabilities.

Latin America has a diverse terrain — from jungles to mountains to plains — posing a challenge in tracking down narcotraffickers on the ground. It’s a task that MQ-9 drones, which are equipped with precision weapons, wide-range sensors and multimode communications suite, can help with.

“Many times these sites are out in the middle of the jungle, and they’re very large scale, like industrial-size sites,” Maltz said. “We know where a lot of these operations are, so they can completely decimate them without putting anybody at risk.”

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said over the weekend that some U.S. troops could be redeployed from Europe to the Western Hemisphere, reiterating the U.S. military is at “war” with drug cartels.

“So we’re going to posture and base as necessary to ensure that we have our foot on the pedal and are taking the fight to those ISIS and Al Qaeda of our hemisphere,” he said Saturday.

There is an effort to surge resources to Southcom, including personnel, assets and other financial resources. Additionally, there have been recent discussions within the Pentagon about moving more troops to the Southcom region, according to the senior Pentagon official.

Adam Isacson, the director for Defense Oversight at the Washington Office on Latin America, said the Pentagon’s drug war will look different than 30 years ago with the joint operations and that U.S. personnel are present in several Latin American countries.

“What could happen, though, is like what happens often, and certainly happened a lot 20 years ago in Colombia, where there’s no formal arrangement, but if you go to many military bases in Colombia at any given moment, then there will be U.S. troops there doing some mission: training, intelligence, logistics, construction.”

U.S. Marines have been at Taura Air Base east of Guayaquil, Ecuador’s biggest city, since August. Marines have launched AeroVironment RQ-20 Puma, a small unmanned aircraft system, for unit-level training.

“Well, we’re conducting joint operations now. We don’t necessarily need to have a base here in order to do that. They had a referendum vote last year,” Secretary of State Marco Rubio said last month during his visit to Ecuador, referring to last year’s referendum in Ecuador in which voters rejected a reversal to a provision that bars building foreign military bases.

Isacson said land strikes are very much a possibility and could come at the border between Ecuador and Colombia.

“I would look for a ramp-up of U.S. assistance and some level of participation in joint operations. If I had to pay money, I would say near the Ecuador border because they’re already doing things on the other side of the Ecuador border, and it’s the same armed groups,” he said.

In late August, U.S. Southern Command (Southcom) Commander, Marine four-star Gen. Francis Donovan met with Colombian Defense Minister Jorge Eduardo Mora in Tumaco, a port city located in the southwest corner of Colombia.

Isacson said those areas are more likely to be targeted than anything near Colombia’s border with Venezuela, where National Liberation Army (ELN), a far-left guerrilla force, is “very good” at bombing oil pipelines.

“If they start kicking the hornets’ nests with the armed groups that operate in the Venezuela border region…those groups could get riled up on the Venezuelan side.”

The Pentagon is looking at the Guatemala-Mexico border and the U.S. border with Mexico as possible areas for future military operations, according to the senior Pentagon official.

“Instead of firing a bunch of arrows and a bunch of targets, you fire a bunch of arrows at the same target, right? And so some of these arrows are law enforcement finishes. Some of these arrows are kinetic finishes. Some of these arrows are maritime strikes,” the official said. “Some of these arrows are land strikes.”

articles.title: AI voice scam traps mom in 5-hour kidnapping nightmare
articles.summary: Deborah Del Mastro heard what sounded like her daughter's terrified voice on the phone, launching a five-hour virtual kidnapping scam ordeal.
articles.body: I want you to think about the voice of someone you love. You know how that person sounds when they're laughing, and you also know the voice you would hear if they were terrified. So what would you do if your phone rang, and you heard that voice begging you for help? That's what happened to Deborah Del Mastro. I recently sat down with Deborah on "The CyberGuy Report" podcast to hear her tell this story in her own words. Even after everything she has been through, you can hear how deeply the experience still affects her. Months after the scam, she also told a U.S. Senate committee that she remained "completely traumatized." The California mother and Navy veteran was having breakfast with her husband when a local number appeared on her phone. The man on the other end claimed a Mexican drug cartel had taken her 37-year-old daughter Sarah. Then Deborah heard the voice that made the threat feel terrifyingly real. "It's my daughter's voice," she told me. "And she's having a panic attack." For the next five and a half hours, the caller threatened Deborah and her family, sent her and her husband from place to place and demanded thousands of dollars. What Deborah didn't know was that the story unfolding on the phone was very different from what was actually happening to Sarah. Join us for a free CyberGuy LIVE class. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson shares practical ways to stay safer, smarter and more confident with technology. Explore classes on stopping spam, phone security, financial protection and using AI to get better healthcare. Each class is free, easy to follow and comes with a free printable checklist. See the classes and register at CyberGuyLive.com THE FAMILY GROUP CHAT IS A GOLDMINE FOR SCAMMERS The phone call that changed everything The call started strangely enough. "I get a local phone call, my area code," Deborah told me. When she answered, the man asked, "Who is this?" Deborah turned the question back on him, and he replied that he was "someone you need to talk to." Then he asked whether Deborah's daughter was prone to panic attacks. That question immediately got her attention. Deborah could hear commotion in the background before the caller put someone else on the line. She heard Sarah. The voice was crying and struggling to breathe. "I'm so sorry, Mom. I'm so scared," Deborah remembers hearing. "It was exactly her voice," she told me. There was another reason Deborah believed she was hearing her daughter. Sarah had recently gone through a breakup, and Deborah had heard her daughter sobbing like that only days earlier. The sound on the phone matched something painfully familiar, which made the call even more convincing. Then came the threat of a Mexican drug cartel The man told Deborah that Sarah had witnessed something she was never supposed to see in a parking lot. He claimed ties to a Mexican drug cartel and said Sarah had her phone out when she saw what happened. According to Deborah, his boss had ordered him to take her. Then he told Deborah what they wanted. "They were going to sell her for $20,000 unless I could come up with the money," Deborah told me. The threat became even darker. She said the caller repeatedly talked about selling Sarah and suggested she could "pay her way in other ways," leaving Deborah terrified that the criminals could sexually traffic her daughter. At that point, she believed violent criminals had Sarah. The scammer made sure Deborah stayed on the phone One of his first instructions was to bring a phone charger. "He tells me that I better charge my phone or bring a phone charger because if my phone dies before we're finished, I'll never see her again," Deborah recalled. That told me a lot about how carefully this scam was run. The caller needed control. He demanded that Deborah keep the phone connected so he could hear what was happening around her. He wanted to know when she moved, what she was doing and who she was talking to. At one point, Deborah muted the call so she could speak privately with her husband. The caller noticed and began screaming. He warned her against trying "funny business." Deborah told me, "He wants to keep my phone open right here so he can hear everything." That control continued for five and a half hours. YOUR FAMILY COULD BE ONE PHONE CALL FROM A BANK SCAM 'Bargaining with the devil' The caller initially wanted $20,000. Deborah didn't have it. "We just don't have that," she remembers telling him. So she started negotiating for what she believed was her daughter's life. "Now I'm bargaining with the devil," she told me. Deborah said she had roughly $2,000 in savings. The caller instructed her to go to a nearby Walmart and use MoneyGram to wire money to Mexico. She went, keeping the phone where he could hear everything happening around her. The man warned that people were watching her in the parking lot and claimed undercover police officers were nearby. He also gave Deborah a story to use if anyone questioned the transfer. The caller told her to say she was helping a relative with medical expenses. "Be discreet," she remembers him telling her. That detail bothers me because scammers often go beyond demanding money. They prepare victims to get around the very people who might recognize that something is wrong. Nobody stopped her Deborah moved from location to location sending money. When I asked whether anyone challenged her or asked whether she was OK, her answer was immediate. "No. No. Not at all." By then, the scammer had already given her a cover story. He had also spent hours convincing Deborah that talking to someone could get Sarah killed. In the end, Deborah sent $5,400 through four separate transactions using MoneyGram and Western Union. She said the transfers took all the accessible money she and her husband had. Later, she put it to me another way: "We were held hostage for 5.5 hours." Deborah and her husband could physically move, but emotionally, the caller had them exactly where he wanted them. Deborah heard Sarah a second time Several hours into the call, Deborah kept asking to speak with her daughter again. Eventually, the caller agreed, but even that conversation came with instructions. He told Deborah exactly what she could say: "This nightmare is nearly over. We're going to come get you as soon as we can." Then Sarah's voice responded. "I'm so sorry, Mom. I love you." I asked Deborah again whether it really sounded like her daughter. "It was her voice," she said. "It was absolutely her voice." Immediately afterward, another man came onto the phone. Deborah described him as an "enforcer" whose threats sounded even harsher. Soon, the scammers demanded more money. A mother was already thinking about her daughter's life afterward There's something Deborah later said that gives you an idea of where her mind had gone during those hours. While her husband drove and the caller listened over the phone, Deborah spent much of the trip sitting silently. Instead of wondering whether this could be a scam, her mind went to Sarah and whether she would survive it. Deborah was already trying to figure out how her daughter would get through life after an experience like this. Paying the ransom was only part of what was running through her mind. She believed something terrible had already happened to her child and started thinking about how she would help Sarah recover afterward. That shows you how completely real this had become to her. The caller finally says Sarah has been released Eventually, the man told Deborah the ordeal was over. He claimed they had released Sarah outside a Walmart where Deborah and her husband were waiting. "Go get her," Deborah remembers him saying. Then he hung up. Deborah could see the front entrance, so she got out of the car and looked for her daughter. Sarah wasn't there. For a moment, Deborah thought the criminals still had her even after taking every dollar she could reach. She frantically looked around before finally calling Sarah herself. Her daughter answered. "Hi, Mom. What's going on?" Sarah was at work. 'I'd never been so relieved to be scammed in my life' For more than five hours, Deborah believed people were holding her daughter and might kill her or sell her. Then Sarah simply answered her phone from work. "I'd never been so relieved to be scammed in my life," Deborah told me. She believes she screamed in the parking lot before the tears came. Deborah told Sarah she loved her, and after work, Sarah came to her parents' home. Her mother hugged her and sobbed. The family then went to the local police department to report what had happened. Losing the money hurt, but Sarah was alive. Sarah immediately suspected an AI voice clone When Deborah explained what had happened, Sarah had an immediate reaction. "Mom, that was probably an AI clone of my voice," Deborah remembers her saying. Both of Deborah's adult children work in IT, so they already knew this kind of technology existed. Deborah didn't. "I didn't know," she recalls. Deborah firmly believes she heard an artificial intelligence-generated version of Sarah's voice. We do know the technology exists, and federal authorities have warned about criminals using it. The FTC says scammers can take a short clip of someone's real voice, including audio posted online, and use voice-cloning technology to make a call sound like that person. How virtual kidnapping scams work The underlying scam has been around much longer than today's AI tools. The FBI calls it "virtual kidnapping." Criminals claim they have taken someone you love even though no kidnapping occurred. One classic warning sign closely matches Deborah's experience. The FBI says virtual kidnappers often work hard to keep victims on the phone so they can't check where their loved one actually is. The agency has also warned about ransom demands involving wire transfers to Mexico. More recently, the FBI warned that criminals are using altered media in virtual kidnapping schemes. AI can make an old scam much more convincing. Deborah put it perfectly: "It is an old scam with new technology." She's a Navy veteran who usually runs toward a crisis One reaction Deborah still encounters is the question some people ask after a scam: Why didn't you hang up? Why didn't you know? Why didn't you tell someone? She understands those questions, but she also knows what was happening inside that call. As a Navy veteran, Deborah describes herself as someone who stays calm in a crisis. "I always say I am the person that runs to the fire, not away from it." Yet the voice on the phone convinced her completely that Sarah was in danger. That's something I want people to remember before judging anyone who falls for one of these calls. You can know about scams and handle pressure well. Then someone puts the terrified voice of your child in your ear. Criminals understand exactly what kind of emotional reaction they're trying to trigger. The financial damage hit hard too The $5,400 represented every readily available dollar Deborah and her husband could access. She says they are seniors living on Social Security along with income from other work, so the loss hit them hard. The following morning, Deborah went to Facebook and told her community what had happened. She also warned that criminals now had "high-tech capability." Friends began sending money, but Deborah initially resisted because she didn't want to profit from what happened. Eventually, they convinced her to create a fundraiser on GoFundMe limited to replacing what the couple had lost. Her community raised the money back. That support couldn't erase the five-and-a-half-hour ordeal, but it meant a great deal to Deborah. Her community had shown up for her before, and they showed up again. 7 ways to protect your family from an AI voice kidnapping scam You don't have to become an expert at detecting synthetic audio. In fact, I wouldn't build your family's defense around your ability to recognize a fake voice. A better approach is to decide now how your family will verify an emergency. 1) Call your loved one yourself If someone claims your child, spouse or another relative has been kidnapped or injured, contact that person directly at the number you already have saved. If they don't answer, try someone who should know where they are. The FTC specifically recommends verifying the story through a phone number you know belongs to your loved one. 2) Create a private family safe word Choose a word or phrase that someone couldn't easily discover through social media. The FBI recommends establishing a family code word for situations like virtual kidnapping scams. Deborah also recommends a safe word now, although her experience shows why you need more than one way to verify an emergency. "There was no way I could have done any of that in this particular situation," she told me. The caller controlled when she could speak with Sarah, so don't make a safe word your family's only verification method. 3) Have another way to verify someone's location After the scam, Deborah and Sarah began using a location-sharing app so each could see where the other was. Apple and Google also offer built-in location-sharing options. If you want to set this up on your phone, see our guide on how to share your whereabouts in any situation using your cell phone. Location sharing comes with its own privacy considerations, so only share your location with people you trust. An agreed-upon way to check someone's whereabouts can give your family another verification tool during an emergency. 4) Pay attention when someone demands secrecy Secrecy played a major role in Deborah's ordeal. The caller told her not to speak to anyone, listened during the transactions and gave her a fake explanation to use if someone asked questions. The FTC says urgency and secrecy are common characteristics of family emergency scams. If someone claims a loved one's survival depends on keeping you from contacting anyone else, treat that as a major warning. 5) Be extremely cautious about wire transfers Scammers like payment methods that move money quickly and make recovery difficult. The FTC specifically warns about emergency scammers demanding wire transfers, cryptocurrency and gift cards. If you've already sent money, contact the bank or transfer company immediately and ask whether it can stop or recall the transaction. Then report what happened to local police and the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center at ic3.gov. 6) Reduce how much personal information criminals can find Your name, relatives, phone numbers and other family connections can appear across people-search sites and data broker databases. That information can make a fake emergency more believable. I've tried manually removing my own information from these sites before, and keeping up with it can turn into a job because the information often returns. A data removal service can help automate some of that work by requesting removal of your information from people-search sites and data broker databases. You can also learn more in our CyberGuy guide on removing your personal information from the web. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com. 7) Talk about this scam before the phone rings This may be the most useful conversation you have with your family this week. Tell them that a familiar voice can be faked. Agree that nobody sends emergency money until someone verifies the situation another way. A few minutes spent setting that expectation today could become extremely important when someone tries to scare you tomorrow. Kurt's key takeaways I've talked with a lot of scam victims over the years, and Deborah's story hit me hard. This wasn't some robotic impersonation that immediately made her suspicious. The voice sounded like her daughter having the kind of panic attack Deborah had heard before. For more than five hours, this guy kept her terrified and focused on one thing: getting Sarah home alive. What stays with me most is where Deborah's mind went during that ordeal. Sitting in the car, she was already wondering how she would help Sarah recover from whatever these supposed kidnappers had done to her. That's a parent's mind at work. The money came later. Sarah came first. I don't think the answer is expecting people to become experts at spotting fake audio. As the technology improves, a convincing voice could fool any of us. Instead, build another way to verify an emergency before one happens. Have a safe word, call your loved one directly and check with someone who may be physically near them. If your family feels comfortable using location sharing, set that up ahead of time. Most importantly, talk about this with the people you love. Deborah had no idea this kind of voice scam was possible before that phone rang. Now she's sharing what happened because she doesn't want another parent sitting in a parking lot wondering whether their child is coming home. Watch or listen to my full conversation with Deborah on The CyberGuy Report podcast at CyberGuy.com. If you heard what sounded exactly like your child or spouse crying and begging you not to hang up, would you remember to verify the call before sending money? What does your family have in place right now? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com. articles.title: WHO questions Russia on reported second plague lab death
articles.summary: The World Health Organization (WHO) is pressing Russia for more information about the unexplained death of a worker at a Siberian plague research institute — and a potential second incident. WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said in a statement Tuesday that the agency has asked Russian authorities to clarify what caused the severe case of…
articles.body:
The World Health Organization (WHO) is pressing Russia for more information about the unexplained death of a worker at a Siberian plague research institute — and a potential second incident.

WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said in a statement Tuesday that the agency has asked Russian authorities to clarify what caused the severe case of pneumonia that killed the 28-year-old worker at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute last week.

“Timely, complete and transparent information sharing under the International Health Regulations is essential to clarify conflicting reports and enable an accurate assessment of potential public health risks,” the statement reads.

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

The worker died Oct. 2 after being hospitalized with severe pneumonia following reports of an alleged accidental lab exposure . Russian authorities have not publicly identified what caused the infection or how she became ill.

The case drew international scrutiny, including from President Trump, who called the case “concerning” and said Tuesday that he planned to speak with Russian President Vladimir Putin about the situation “very soon.”

According to Ghebreyesus, Russian health authorities told the WHO that no plague cases have recently been recorded in the Irkutsk region and that an epidemiological investigation was conducted.

Officials said contacts of the worker were tested and placed under medical observation, with no high-threat pathogens detected , and preventative and control measures had been implemented. Roughly 200 people were initially quarantined as authorities investigated the death.

The WHO chief said his organization has remained in contact with Russian officials and offered technical support but is seeking additional information about the cause of the worker’s pneumonia, the pathogen that prompted the public health response and reports involving a second employee.

Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov disputed reports surrounding the incident, saying the “vast majority” of media coverage about the situation was false and directing people to information provided by Russian public health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor.

Peskov also pushed back on Trump saying there was a scheduled phone call with Putin to discuss the matter, saying no such conversation had been scheduled.

articles.body:
The execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, who was convicted of killing 13 people in the 2009 Fort Hood mass shooting, is set for December, according to the U.S. Army.

The Tuesday memo, obtained by The Hill’s partner network NewsNation, lists the time as Dec. 3 at 1 p.m. CDT. It will be carried out at the Fort Hood base in Central Texas.

On Monday, Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell announced on social platform X that Hasan was sentenced to death by firing squad. Parnell, who has been floated as the next Army secretary, said Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth “recommended” the death penalty and President Trump “approved it.”

“Secretary of War Pete Hegseth has recommended — and President Donald J. Trump has approved — death by U.S. Army firing squad for convicted terrorist Nidal Malik Hasan, the jihadist who opened fire on unarmed American soldiers at Fort Hood in 2009,” Parnell said in his post.

Hasan is a convicted terrorist who opened fire on unarmed American soldiers at the base, killing 13 people and injuring 32 others. During the incident, the ex-Army psychiatrist was heard shouting, “Allahu Akbar.”

During the 2013 trial, Hasan opted to represent himself, saying in his opening statement that “the evidence will clearly show that I am the shooter.”

He later added the evidence would find “that we are imperfect Muslims trying to establish the perfect religion … I apologize for any mistakes I made in this endeavor.”

Hasan said he carried out the shooting in response to the U.S. wars in Iraq and Afghanistan. The incident came one month before the then-soldier was scheduled to deploy to Afghanistan.

articles.title: OpenAI releases new batch of math breakthroughs
articles.summary: OpenAI released a new batch of mathematics breakthroughs on Tuesday following calls from AI researchers and developers to slow the growth of the technology. The company released 377 results that cover physics, mathematical and other scientific problems solved by an OpenAI internal frontier model not yet available to the public. “Towards acceleration of scientific discovery…
articles.body:
OpenAI released a new batch of mathematics breakthroughs on Tuesday following calls from AI researchers and developers to slow the growth of the technology.

The company released 377 results that cover physics, mathematical and other scientific problems solved by an OpenAI internal frontier model not yet available to the public.

“Towards acceleration of scientific discovery and improving quality of life for everyone,” OpenAI’s president and co-founder Greg Brockman wrote on social media about the findings.

In response to previous solutions , the tech firm faced backlash from prominent mathematicians over whether the solution the AI model created was original or plagiarized the work of other human mathematicians.

On the same day, OpenAI put together an independent advisory group of mathematicians to “develop best practices, and we have drawn on their advice and public recommendations to inform how we release these results.”

Harvard University mathematics professor Melanie Matchett Wood, one member of the advisory board, stated, “AI systems are able to give a lot of output that is mathematical in some ways, but is not conforming to important academic standards,” according to the Harvard Crimson .

“It often includes plagiarism. It fails to present ideas clearly, fails to document the entire scientific process, and usually there’s no human who is willing to take responsibility for the output,” she continued.

Their new guidelines , which helped to shape the release of the batch, included requiring papers generated by frontier models to be understandable by human standards, releasing the chain of thought leading to the breakthrough and citing the papers in which certain ideas were first introduced.

The advisory group noted it was up to mathematicians to determine whether OpenAI had fully implemented its voluntary recommendations in this batch.

The findings come after multiple incidents of OpenAI models going “rogue” and compromising Modal Labs and Hugging Face systems in separate attacks. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman called for a slowdown in development to manage the technology’s risks.

The company also halted the release of its newest model — called GPT-6.1 Astra — as it “didn’t quite meet the bar in terms of staying within scope authorization, and how it communicates back to the user about the type of work it’s done,” according to a statement to The Hill, citing the company’s head of safety systems, Saachi Jain.

articles.title: Rand Paul concerned Russian plague could be ‘weaponized’
articles.summary: Sen. Rand Paul (R-Ky.) raised concerns that Russia could be conducting biological weapons research involving the plague as global health officials seek more information about the mysterious death of a worker at a Siberian lab. The 28-year-old worker died Friday after being hospitalized from a severe case of pneumonia, prompting the World Health Organization to…
articles.body:
Sen. Rand Paul (R-Ky.) raised concerns that Russia could be conducting biological weapons research involving the plague as global health officials seek more information about the mysterious death of a worker at a Siberian lab.

The 28-year-old worker died Friday after being hospitalized from a severe case of pneumonia, prompting the World Health Organization to seek further information from Russian authorities on her unexplained death and a potential second incident.

Paul, who chairs the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, said in an interview Tuesday that Russia’s past biological weapons program and the circumstances surrounding the worker’s death warranted closer scrutiny.

“We do know from defectors in the 1970s and ‘80s that they were weaponizing the plague,” the senator told Fox News’s Will Cain. “So, this is concerning.”

Paul did not provide evidence of his claims or confirm that the worker’s death was connected to a biological weapons program. He suggested, however, that U.S. officials examine satellite imagery and Russian military activity for signs of anything unusual.

“It looks like some people are insinuating there is more activity than you would normally get from one case of the plague,” the Kentucky Republican continued, “which makes us concerned, could it be weaponized?”

Daria Shipilova, an employee at an anti-plague research facility in Russia’s Irkutsk region, reportedly died after breaking a test tube containing live bacteria on Sept. 25.

Irkutsk region Governor Igor Kobzev said the employee died of “pneumonia of unknown etiology,” prompting the investigation and isolation of nearly 200 people who may have potentially been exposed.

Paul called Russia’s lack of clarity about the case of death “alarming,” arguing that officials should be able to quickly determine whether the plague was responsible for the death.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said it was aware of the incident and is “closely monitoring reports of a suspected case of pneumonic plague,” adding there currently is no indication of a broader threat to the U.S.

“Pneumonic plague can spread person-to-person through respiratory droplets during close contact, which is why rapid identification and treatment of infected individuals, and monitoring of potentially exposed individuals, are important public health measures,” the agency said in a statement.

articles.title: AI safety group outlines demands for legislation, warns lawmakers
articles.summary: Guardrails Action, a nonprofit pushing for safeguards on artificial intelligence, led a coalition of nearly 40 organizations to outline a series of key principles for AI legislation, warning that it will oppose anything less. In a Wednesday letter to lawmakers, the coalition argued legislation must feature enforceable and transparent government oversight that is not designed…
articles.body:
Guardrails Action, a nonprofit pushing for safeguards on artificial intelligence, led a coalition of nearly 40 organizations to outline a series of key principles for AI legislation , warning that it will oppose anything less.

In a Wednesday letter to lawmakers, the coalition argued legislation must feature enforceable and transparent government oversight that is not designed or controlled by major tech firms.

It also said AI rules should have a broad mandate covering everything from existential risks to economic shocks and should be judged by their impact on humanity rather than stock performance, in addition to calling for the enforcement of existing laws.

“The public is demanding action on AI,” the group continued. “Any AI regulatory legislation that fails to meet the above basic principles will not receive our support; it will be met with active, mobilized opposition. This moment requires nothing less.”

Guardrails Action was joined in the letter by several major unions and advocacy groups, including the American Federation of Teachers, End Citizens United, National Education Association, Public Citizen, Tech Oversight Project and United Auto Workers.

It comes at a moment when numerous AI-related cybersecurity incidents and dire warnings from researchers have prompted some AI leaders to call for a slowdown in development and seek guardrails on the technology.

“Big AI and their army of lobbyists and publicists want to divide Congress and the public on this issue. The public isn’t fooled and Congress shouldn’t be either,” said Shaunna Thomas, executive director of Guardrails Action, in a statement.

“The American public is demanding guardrails to keep themselves and their families safe, accountability for the ways the technology sector has already caused harm, and leadership that puts human beings at the center of the conversation,” she added.

The nonprofit and its associated super PAC, Guardrails Alliance, launched earlier this year as part of an effort to push for AI regulation and counter the spending of Leading the Future, an AI industry-backed super PAC.

Guardrails Alliance separately announced Wednesday that it plans to spend $1.2 million opposing three candidates backed by Leading the Future — including Republican candidates Aaron Flint and Jay Feely, who are running in Montana and Arizona, respectively, and Rep. Jimmy Gomez (D-Calif.).

articles.title: Truck stops warned against red-dyed diesel sales: ‘Limited upside’
articles.summary: Truck stops were warned by industry groups against selling red-dyed diesel, saying there is “limited upside” to its sale following reported record-high diesel prices across the U.S. “The White House appears to be trying to encourage the supply chain to move toward selling dyed fuel in non-traditional ways,” the Society of Independent Gasoline Marketers of…
articles.body:
Truck stops were warned by industry groups against selling red-dyed diesel , saying there is “limited upside” to its sale following reported record-high diesel prices across the U.S.

“The White House appears to be trying to encourage the supply chain to move toward selling dyed fuel in non-traditional ways,” the Society of Independent Gasoline Marketers of America (SIGMA) and the National Association of Truck Stop Owners (NATSO) said in a note to their members, according to NBC News . “We do not expect most reputable diesel retailers and fuel marketers to do this … first, the tax is still owed, so there’s limited upside.”

SIGMA and NATSO added, “The logistical challenges outweigh any visible upside: Residual dye lingers in tanks and fuel systems.”

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

They concluded that for fuel sellers the “liability and customer risk outweigh any temporary, uncertain benefit,” per NBC News.

President Trump announced earlier this week various directives aiming to increase the availability of red-dyed diesel and lower diesel prices. This diesel simply has red dye added to it to signal that it is tax exempt and is typically used in machines such as farm and construction equipment.

The coloring also helps “law enforcement … identify it to enforce penalties and back taxes for on-road use,” a fact sheet from the White House explains.

Under the executive order, the red-dye diesel tax is “deferred,” halting enforcement by the IRS from Oct. 5 to Dec. 13, according to a White House official. The order directed the IRS to “explore avenues, including legislation, to eliminate the obligation to pay” the deferred taxes.

The official continued that the Treasury Department and the IRS are preparing guidance on tax relief related to this order for taxpayers to reference.

Another group, Energy Marketers of America, criticized the order and warned gas stations to “proceed with caution,” according to NBC News.

“Whether relief is available, whom it covers, and on what conditions depend on Treasury determinations and guidance not yet issued,” the group said. “Deferral is not forgiveness.”

When asked about the industry group’s remarks, White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers said, “President Trump’s executive action will quickly cut diesel costs by authorizing highway use of tax-free dyed diesel and deferring the federal diesel excise tax through the end of the year.”

“This will put money directly back into the pockets of American truckers, farmers, and workers—providing savings of as much as $100 per fill,” she continued.
