articles.title: Doxxing Jane Doe
articles.summary: X and Substack aren’t doing anything to stop users from harassing women they believe are connected to the rape case — and the women who aren’t.﻿
articles.body: Who is Jane Doe? Online vigilantes have tried to expose the Cornell University student who filed a lawsuit accusing seven fraternity members of gang rape, and in so doing have invited a torrent of abuse on several other women. Her lawyers say three women have been falsely identified and harassed — and the real Jane Doe is being inundated with threats, too. “She’s not doing well,” her attorney Thomas Guiffra told CNN on Sunday. “She’s under siege on social media, where people are trying to identify her.” The fact several women are now facing a torrent of online abuse in connection to Jane Doe’s lawsuit isn’t surprising. Targeted harassment and intimidation campaigns were a hallmark of the backlash to #MeToo. These targeted harassment campaigns were once organized on websites like Kiwi Farms and 4chan. But the effort to unmask Jane Doe — and to terrorize any woman they believe to be Jane Doe — is happening right in the open, on mainstream social media platforms that aren’t doing anything to stop it. Jane Doe’s identity isn’t a total secret: It’s known to her attorneys, the judge presiding over the case, the seven men she’s accusing of rape, and their attorneys, too. In civil cases, a plaintiff’s anonymity is ultimately up to the judge, who weighs several factors, including whether identifying the plaintiff by name will put them at risk of physical or mental injury. “In New York, there’s no automatic right to proceed anonymously,” said Annie Seifullah, a founding partner at the victims’ rights firm Incendii Law. Still, “the law recognizes that survivors’ lives are routinely put on trial, and that forcing them to sue under their real names would keep many victims of sexual violence from coming forward at all.” Similarly, journalistic ethics guides typically suggest showing sensitivity to victims of alleged sex crimes, and reporters will often allow people alleging abuse to do so anonymously, so long as their identity can be independently corroborated. The attempt to expose Jane Doe began on X, where Substack author and podcast host Michael Tracey — who is perhaps best known for his skepticism toward the allegations made about Jeffrey Epstein — solicited information about her. Tracey said he considered her identity fair game “since her lawsuit didn’t hesitate to name & shame 7 of her peers as gang-rapists.” Aidan Thompson, founder of the AF Post — a publication dedicated to articulating “the ideas, beliefs, and values of the America First Movement” — also asked for help identifying Jane Doe. “Beev, please help me discover the Cornell girl,” he posted on September 29th, referring to the “burnerverse,” a network of anonymous X accounts whose members discuss college sports and wage harassment campaigns against women with equal zeal. “The fact that people are trying so hard to dox her and are harassing her and others — women they just think might be her — underscores how serious her privacy interest really is,” said Katie McKay, a senior associate at C.A. Goldberg, a victims’ rights firm that specializes in tech-facilitated abuse. “Obviously the anonymity is necessary. It’s protecting her, to some extent, from even more harassment, even more targeting and retaliation.” X’s terms of service expressly prohibits users from sharing a person’s private information without their consent, and from threatening to do so; the site has also banned people who post the alleged names of pseudonymous users. But non-users’ names and photos aren’t considered “private information,” even if they can be used to dig up actual private details like their phone number or home address. X’s rules also say users “may not target others with abuse or harassment, or encourage other people to do so,” but the platform is flooded with posts disparaging women believed to be Jane Doe. X did not respond to a request for comment. On X, Thompson posted photos and biographical details of a woman he claimed was Jane Doe. Tracey later identified the same woman as Jane Doe on his Substack, claiming to have seen her name on court records. In fact, Tracey got the name from a court records aggregator — a website that, according to disinformation researcher Jared Holt, was registered in mid-September and seems to selectively post information about polarizing cases, like Clavicular’s and Lindsay Clancy’s. Despite Tracey’s repeated assertions that Jane Doe’s identity was a matter of public interest, many comments on his Substack post focused on the purported Jane Doe’s sex appeal and how this related to the veracity of her allegations. On X, dozens if not hundreds of people — ranging from anonymous accounts to prominent right-wing commentators — are now scrutinizing her appearance, making sexual comments about her, and disparaging her boyfriend. Anonymous accounts have circulated her Instagram and TikTok posts and made AI deepfakes of the woman Tracey and Thompson named. Substack, too, is known for its lax content moderation policies. The platform has taken a laissez-faire approach to publishing, and in 2023 infamously refused to remove or demonetize several Nazi publications from its website. Tracey has seemingly benefited from his posts about Jane Doe: Substack lists his newsletter as 66th on its politics leaderboard. Substack did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Tracey, for his part, deleted the post in which he claimed to have identified Jane Doe — not because of his shoddy sourcing but because he claimed to have made his point: High-profile litigants shouldn’t be allowed to be anonymous, especially when accusing others of rape. “That’s all I ever sought to accomplish here,” he wrote. “Not to impugn this young woman on a personal level. I have no animus toward her, and never have. I sincerely wish her the best, and hope her life is not defined by this calamity.” Tracey did not respond to a request for comment. Jane Doe isn’t anonymous to the court. “Underlying this is the belief that it’s somehow unfair to these defendants that she’s anonymous and they’re not. But they know who she is,” McKay said. “I don’t see a lack of accountability, even as a Jane Doe, in voluntarily subjecting your claims to the scrutiny of a court, with the subpoena power and the discovery power of the court.” Because the defendants know Jane Doe’s identity, their attorneys will be able to request access to her medical records, psychiatric records, and personal communications. “If the worry is that she wouldn’t be held accountable for any kind of false allegation, the whole process is designed to vet these allegations and only allow the claim to move forward — and her to potentially recover anything — if it’s deemed meritorious upon examination of all this evidence.” And regardless of their stated motivations for doing so, anyone who has spent any time on X since 2022 (or the internet more broadly) would know that identifying a woman as Jane Doe would inevitably result in that woman getting a torrent of abuse. Either Thompson and Tracey identified and directed harassment toward an alleged rape victim, or they directed harassment toward an unrelated woman in their quest to expose the identity of an alleged rape victim. These harassment campaigns reverberate beyond their intended targets, creating a broader culture of intimidation. “I’ve already had many clients call me to ask if they should be worried about being doxxed over their Jane Doe status,” said Seifullah, the victims’ rights attorney. “Most survivors don’t report and this is why.” Ironically, Tracey is now complaining that an online mob is not only going after his family but also targeting the new owners of his childhood home, to which he has no relation. Harassment of people who come forward with sexual assault allegations isn’t a new phenomenon, andbut McKay noted that stringent efforts were taken to protect the identity of Emily Doe, woman who accused Stanford swimmer Brock Turner of rape in 2015, and “I don’t recall much of a doxxing campaign,” McKay said — even after Emily Doe’s victim impact statement went viral. When Chanel Miller came forward four years later, the news of her identity was truly revelatory even to those who had criticized her during Turner’s high-profile trial. “I think the interest in ‘exposing’ victims is going to be magnified these days,” McKay said. Though it’s impossible to pinpoint what changed, McKay pointed to harassment campaigns directed at Amber Heard and E. Jean Carroll, two women who publicly accused famous men of rape. “Those women were publicly identified, and they were torn to shreds, viciously attacked by the public,” McKay said. “I don’t know if perhaps that’s created more of an interest or an expectation that every case is going to let observers who are non-litigants pick apart the victim, but it seems pretty clear to me that’s what they want to do here.” [Media: Just like the #MeToo movement encouraged women to share their stories, the attempt to expose Jane Doe has generated a new wave of solidarity. On TikTok and Instagram, hundreds of women responded to Tracey’s request for information about the alleged Cornell victim with an “I am Spartacus”-esque campaign in which they proclaim to be Jane Doe. Some women are even coming forward with their own stories of sexual assault. Sarah Lupica, a 24-year-old content creator with more than 1.5 million followers on TikTok, posted a video about being sexually assaulted when she was 16 years old. “For the longest time, I blamed myself for being in that situation,” Lupica told me. Until now, she said, she lacked the language to explain what happened to her. Lupica was 13 years old at the height of #MeToo and had no recollection of the movement. It didn’t reach her. The moment passed, the culture changed, and the abuse of women persisted in a culture that is even more hostile to survivors. For Lupica, #IAmJaneDoe is a way of not only sharing her own story but showing other women that they aren’t alone. Lupica said she felt emboldened by the amount of other women who were coming forward. “I was really touched by it, and the whole movement of saying ‘I am Jane Doe,’” she told me. “It’s saying you stand with her and with everyone who’s been scared to speak — survivors who never got justice and girls who are really trying to understand what happened to them.”

articles.title: Most say Trump, Congress not taking AI risk seriously: Survey
articles.summary: Most U.S. voters want more safeguards on artificial intelligence and think the federal government has fallen short in confronting the powerful technology’s risks, according to a new poll. In a Reuters/Ipsos survey released Wednesday, 57 percent of respondents said they believe the Trump administration is not taking the risks posed by AI seriously enough, while…
articles.body:
Most U.S. voters want more safeguards on artificial intelligence and think the federal government has fallen short in confronting the powerful technology’s risks, according to a new poll.

In a Reuters/Ipsos survey released Wednesday, 57 percent of respondents said they believe the Trump administration is not taking the risks posed by AI seriously enough, while 54 percent said the same of Congress.

Concerns extended across party lines. Eighty percent of Democrats and 61 percent of Republicans said they support stricter government regulation of AI.

The findings come as the rapid expansion of AI has increasingly collided with concerns over job security, energy costs and public safety — issues campaigns are working to address ahead of next month’s midterm elections.

Following several incidents of AI models going rogue and breaching other systems without authorization, including OpenAI’s incident with Hugging Face and federal government websites, nearly two-thirds of voters said they believe AI could eventually spiral beyond human control.

President Trump, who recently dubbed the technology “superintelligence,” has dismissed concerns about the technology and the need to impose stricter rules.

Trump has pushed for rapid development of AI and the data centers needed to power it, arguing the U.S. risks losing ground to China in the global race for AI dominance if it places too many restrictions on the industry.

The poll found opposition to the rapid construction of data centers, with 56 percent of voters saying they support limits on new data center construction, including 69 percent of Democrats and 43 percent of Republicans.

The Trump administration has largely favored voluntary safeguards over sweeping federal regulations. Last week, Trump announced that executives from the world’s leading tech companies, including Nvidia, SpaceX, Meta, Anthropic and Google, had agreed to a “morally-binding” self-policing pledge that involved a series of safety measures, including external reviews of their AI systems.

According to the survey, voters were particularly concerned about the technology’s effect on the job market. Eighty-four percent said AI poses a threat to American workers, compared with 74 percent who said the same about competition from foreign workers and 60 percent who viewed illegal immigration as a threat to U.S. workers.

In a statement to Reuters, a White House official pointed to a newly created AI task force aimed at maintaining U.S. leadership in the technology. The official also told the outlet that the administration is focused on creating a strong economy that can withstand what they described as potential short-term disruptions to the workforce.

articles.title: What is kratom, herb drawing scrutiny from lawmakers?
articles.summary: Kratom, a plant with opioid-like properties sold over the counter, has drawn growing scrutiny from lawmakers on Capitol Hill as some states seek to ban the product or its synthetic derivatives. Calls for a federal response, including Sen. Chuck Grassley’s (R-Iowa) request that the Trump administration act, come after compounds of kratom were found in…
articles.body:
Kratom, a plant with opioid-like properties sold over the counter, has drawn growing scrutiny from lawmakers on Capitol Hill as some states seek to ban the product or its synthetic derivatives .

Calls for a federal response, including Sen. Chuck Grassley’s (R-Iowa) request that the Trump administration act, come after compounds of kratom were found in connection with the deaths of two University of Mississippi students last month.

Kratom-related exposure reports went up by 1,200 percent from 2015 to 2025, according to a March report from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, though overdoses and deaths connected to the plant are rare.

The National Institute on Drug Abuse (NIDA) describes kratom, or Mitragyna speciosa, as an herbal substance related to the coffee family and originating from tropical trees in Southeast Asia.

It can produce “opioid- and stimulant-like effects” and can be used to manage drug withdrawal symptoms and cravings, as well as to ease conditions like chronic pain, anxiety, depression, coughing and diarrhea.

The substance, typically sold in capsule and powder form, contains the well-studied chemical compounds mitragynine and 7-hydroxymitragynine (7-OH). Kratom interacts with the human brain similarly to how chocolate, coffee and exercise do through receptor sites in the brain.

Although 7-OH naturally occurs within kratom, the synthetic form can be 13 times more potent than morphine, a Schedule II narcotic in the U.S., and contains as much as 500 percent more 7-OH than the herb contains naturally, according to the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in 2025 .

The FDA has not approved any uses of kratom, while the NIDA warns that some kratom users reported feeling dizzy, nauseated, drowsy and constipated after using the product.

Grassley on Friday called on the Trump administration to finalize the Drug Enforcement Administration’s (DEA) proposed rule to ban any synthetic kratom.

The Iowa Republican warned against kratom, calling it “special interest snake oil.” He said the plant should not be made available at gas stations, vape shops or “ANYWHERE.”

Other Republican lawmakers warned against kratom’s effects, with Sen. Pete Ricketts (R-Neb.) calling kratom products “highly addictive and can be laced with even deadlier drugs.”

“This poison is being falsely marketed as a supplement when, in reality, it’s a dangerous drug killing children and destroying the lives of so many families,” Rep. Andy Harris (R-Md.) wrote Friday on the social platform X . “FDA and DEA need to act NOW.”

Rep. Mike Levin (D-Calif.) accused the administration of corruption over Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin’s reported support for the kratom industry. The New York Times obtained a disclosure statement listing Mullin as having as much as $1 million invested in kratom company Botanic Tonics.

“When Mullin was a senator, he pushed the FDA on kratom’s behalf, urging the agency to scrub safety warnings from its website,” Levin wrote in June on X . “Then, after Trump nominated him to lead DHS, the Justice Department dropped its lawsuit against the company he holds investments in, and he STILL hasn’t divested.”

The Department of Homeland Security said in response to the Times’s reporting that Mullin “follows all ethics and conflict of interest standards and has not lobbied for any individual or company.”

The DEA published its proposed rule to temporarily ban certain synthetic versions of kratom in July.

It would classify kratom products as Schedule I substances if they contain more than 0.05 percent dry weight of 7-OH and would allow the milder version of the plant “to continue flying under regulatory radar,” health news outlet Stat reported last month.

The agency also temporarily scheduled three 7-OH-related substances found online in candies, tablets and liquid shots. The DEA said MP, MGM-15 and MGM-16 are marketed as kratom extracts when they actually contain synthetic opioid compounds and do not occur naturally. In August, the DEA announced emergency scheduling of MGM-15 and MGM-16.

Though the DEA lists kratom as a “drug of concern,” these changes did not impact that. The agency specified that it was not seeking to regulate botanical kratom products.

The proposed rule has not been finalized. If it is, it would remain in effect for up to two years, with the chance to be extended if the DEA chooses to pursue a permanent scheduling.

Compounds of kratom found in connection with student deaths

In September, two students at the University of Mississippi were found dead in a dorm room with “packaged kratom” bought from a retail store identified by investigators, according to the Lafayette County Metro Narcotics team .

The kratom found with the students contained 7-OH, MP and MGM-15, CNN reported , citing court documents.

None of the compounds have been confirmed as causing or contributing to the deaths of freshman Aidan Hamilton and junior Robert Strang. Autopsy results from the Lafayette County coroner remain pending, according to Memphis-based Nexstar affiliate WREG .

Shawnboda Mead, the University of Mississippi’s vice chancellor for student affairs, warned against “inaccurate information” about Hamilton and Strang’s deaths “being shared by individuals who do not have access to the facts.”

“We can all help by not repeating information that has not been officially confirmed and by avoiding public speculation about what happened or why, especially as the causes of the two deaths are still under investigation,” Mead said.

The substance largely remains legal across the U.S., though 108 out of around 400 state bills on kratom proposed banning the substance, according to an analysis from The Washington Post . Another 258 bills set limitations and requirements, such as age and potency limits, that ban synthetic kratom but keep natural kratom legal.

Kratom has been fully banned in nine states: Alabama, Arkansas, Connecticut, Indiana, Vermont, Louisiana, Tennessee and Wisconsin, with Massachusetts being the most recent state to join the list in August.

State lawmakers in Washington, Michigan and South Carolina have proposed banning the substance, and Rhode Island reversed its ban to make the product legal for adults 21 years and older.

articles.title: Supreme Court weighs case over Air Force detonating munitions in Guam
articles.summary: The Supreme Court on Wednesday wrestled with a case about whether the Air Force needs to conduct environmental review before its munitions detonations in Guam. An environmental group, Prutehi Guåhan, has sued, saying that the decision to file a permit renewal application with the Guam Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) constitutes an agency action that triggered…
articles.body:
The Supreme Court on Wednesday wrestled with a case about whether the Air Force needs to conduct environmental review before its munitions detonations in Guam.

An environmental group, Prutehi Guåhan, has sued, saying that the decision to file a permit renewal application with the Guam Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) constitutes an agency action that triggered environmental review, noting that the move to submit the renewal application automatically allowed the Air Force to continue operating under the prior permit.

The Ninth Circuit court of appeals agreed with Prutehi Guåhan.

The Air Force, however, has asked the court to overturn that decision. It argues both that a decision to file a permit application is not a final agency action subject to judicial review and that since it is seeking the permit under the nation’s hazardous waste law, it does not have to conduct an environmental review under a separate statute known as the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA).

NEPA requires the government to consider environmental consequences of major federal actions before they are carried out.

The case could have broader implications for whether the U.S. government, including the military, needs to conduct environmental reviews of certain actions that are assessed by a separate authority such as the Guam EPA.

The justices asked tough questions of both the Air Force and Prutehi Guåhan, not giving a clear indication of which way they would rule.

However, in a case last term, the court narrowed the scope of environmental reviews under NEPA , and its conservative justices may not want to expand the jurisdiction of the environmental statute.

The justices questioned the Air Force’s logic that the application to renew its detonation permit is not an agency action, asking whether opponents could ever sue to stop it.

“So you’re saying that there’s no point at which the Air Force’s decision can be challenged because even if Guam goes ahead and says, ‘OK, you know, granted,’ you’re saying you don’t have to go forward with it. You could always change your mind. You could say, ‘Oh, OK, now we’re going to do something different.’ The Air Force’s action is never final and therefore never reviewable,” said Chief Justice John Roberts.

“I’m not seeing how it would make any sense to say that it’s not final, but then that NEPA still applies, which is a possible outcome here,” added Justice Brett Kavanaugh.

However, the justices also questioned the environmental organization about whether deciding that the application is a final challengeable action could have broader implications for permit applications.

“If we say that this is final agency action, what ramifications do you think this would have in the more normal situation where, to the extent the government is the one who’s the regulated entity seeking a permit, appearing before EPA or some other like you know service transportation board or something like that, would this have a big impact or no?” asked Justice Amy Coney Barrett.

“I don’t think that this is going to open the floodgates to more attacks on permitting decisions,” responded attorney Caroline Flynn, who represented Prutehi Guåhan.

The justices also asked tough questions of both sides on whether the fact that the Air Force was seeking a permit under the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act, which governs hazardous waste disposal, necessarily excluded NEPA review.

They asked the government about provisions in NEPA that say a review has to be completed unless the review would conflict with another law.

“It doesn’t say expressly excluded,” Justice Department lawyer Sopan Joshi told the court.

“So it’s implicitly excluded?” asked Justice Neil Gorsuch. “How is it implicitly excluded?”

“Under the specific-general canon. That is a well-known doctrine of law in which a more specific statute …,” Joshi replied.

“OK, but if I disagree with you about that?” asked Gorsuch.

They questioned Flynn on the same issue.

“Do you think our case law supports the proposition that a newer statute that deals very extensively with a specific problem cannot displace an older statute that deals with a much broader range of activities only if it is impossible to comply with both of those statutes?” asked Justice Samuel Alito.

“I do. I think this court’s cases have required a conflict,” Flynn responded.

“Do you think that the duty to harmonize is consistent with the requirement that it must be absolutely impossible to comply with both?” Alito pressed.
